notes.front: Which fabric patches are preventive maintenance under Appendix A(c)?
notes.back: Simple patches not requiring rib stitching or removal of structural parts or control surfaces.
notes.explanation: Item (7) also allows small balloon envelope repairs that need no load tape repair or replacement.
notes.evidence: (7) Making simple fabric patches not requiring rib stitching or the removal of structural parts or control surfaces.

notes.front: Where may hydraulic fluid be replenished as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: In the hydraulic reservoir.
notes.explanation: Item (8) of Appendix A(c) lists replenishing it there.
notes.evidence: (8) Replenishing hydraulic fluid in the hydraulic reservoir.

notes.front: Refinishing the decorative coating of which tail group surfaces is excluded from preventive maintenance item (9)?
notes.back: Balanced control surfaces.
notes.explanation: Item (9) also requires that no removal or disassembly of primary structure or operating systems is needed.
notes.evidence: (9) Refinishing decorative coating of fuselage, balloon baskets, wings tail group surfaces (excluding balanced control surfaces), fairings, cowlings,

notes.front: When is applying preservative or protective material to components preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When no primary structure or operating system is disassembled, and the coating is not prohibited or contrary to good practice.
notes.explanation: Item (10) sets both conditions.
notes.evidence: (10) Applying preservative or protective material to components where no disassembly of any primary structure or operating system is involved and where such coating is not prohibited or is not contrary to good practices.

notes.front: When is repairing cabin upholstery and decorative furnishings preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When it needs no disassembly of primary structure or operating systems and does not interfere with them.
notes.explanation: Item (11) covers the cabin, cockpit or balloon basket interior.
notes.evidence: (11) Repairing upholstery and decorative furnishings of the cabin, cockpit, or balloon basket interior when the repairing does not require disassembly of any primary structure or operating system

notes.front: Which repairs to fairings, cover plates and cowlings are preventive maintenance under item (12)?
notes.back: Small simple repairs, and small patches and reinforcements not changing the contour so as to interfere with proper airflow.
notes.explanation: The cover plates must be nonstructural.
notes.evidence: (12) Making small simple repairs to fairings, nonstructural cover plates, cowlings, and small patches and reinforcements not changing the contour so as to interfere with proper air flow.

notes.front: When is replacing side windows preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When the work does not interfere with the structure or any operating system.
notes.explanation: Item (13) gives controls and electrical equipment as examples of operating systems.
notes.evidence: (13) Replacing side windows where that work does not interfere with the structure or any operating system such as controls, electrical equipment, etc.

notes.front: Is replacing safety belts preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Yes: item (14) of Appendix A(c).
notes.explanation: It is listed without further condition, between side windows and seats.
notes.evidence: (13) Replacing side windows where that work does not interfere with the structure or any operating system such as controls, electrical equipment, etc. (14) Replacing safety belts.

notes.front: When is replacing seats or seat parts preventive maintenance?
notes.back: With replacement parts approved for the aircraft, not involving disassembly of primary structure or operating systems.
notes.explanation: Item (15) sets both conditions.
notes.evidence: (15) Replacing seats or seat parts with replacement parts approved for the aircraft, not involving disassembly of any primary structure or operating system.

notes.front: Which wiring may be troubleshot and repaired as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Broken circuits in landing light wiring circuits.
notes.explanation: Item (16) is limited to landing light circuits.
notes.evidence: (16) Trouble shooting and repairing broken circuits in landing light wiring circuits.

notes.front: Which light parts may be replaced as preventive maintenance under item (17)?
notes.back: Bulbs, reflectors and lenses of position and landing lights.
notes.explanation: Item (17) covers these three parts of those two kinds of light.
notes.evidence: (17) Replacing bulbs, reflectors, and lenses of position and landing lights.

notes.front: When is replacing wheels and skis preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When no weight and balance computation is involved.
notes.explanation: Item (18) of Appendix A(c) sets this condition.
notes.evidence: (18) Replacing wheels and skis where no weight and balance computation is involved.

notes.front: When is replacing a cowling preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When it does not require removing the propeller or disconnecting flight controls.
notes.explanation: Item (19) of Appendix A(c) sets these limits.
notes.evidence: (19) Replacing any cowling not requiring removal of the propeller or disconnection of flight controls.

notes.front: Which spark plug tasks are preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting spark plug gap clearance.
notes.explanation: Item (20) of Appendix A(c) lists them.
notes.evidence: (20) Replacing or cleaning spark plugs and setting of spark plug gap clearance.

notes.front: Which hose connections are excluded from preventive maintenance item (21)?
notes.back: Hydraulic connections.
notes.explanation: Item (21) otherwise allows replacing any hose connection.
notes.evidence: (21) Replacing any hose connection except hydraulic connections.

notes.front: Which fuel lines may be replaced as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Prefabricated fuel lines.
notes.explanation: Item (22) of Appendix A(c) is limited to prefabricated lines.
notes.evidence: (22) Replacing prefabricated fuel lines.

notes.front: Which fuel and oil items may be cleaned or replaced as preventive maintenance under item (23)?
notes.back: Fuel and oil strainers or filter elements.
notes.explanation: Item (23) of Appendix A(c) lists them.
notes.evidence: (23) Cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers or filter elements.

notes.front: Is replacing and servicing batteries preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Yes: item (24) of Appendix A(c).
notes.explanation: It is listed without further condition.
notes.evidence: (23) Cleaning or replacing fuel and oil strainers or filter elements. (24) Replacing and servicing batteries.

notes.front: Which balloon burner parts may be cleaned as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: The burner pilot and main nozzles, following the balloon manufacturer's instructions.
notes.explanation: Item (25) of Appendix A(c) lists this.
notes.evidence: (25) Cleaning of balloon burner pilot and main nozzles in accordance with the balloon manufacturer's instructions.

notes.front: Which fasteners may be replaced or adjusted as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Nonstructural standard fasteners incidental to operations.
notes.explanation: Item (26) of Appendix A(c) lists them.
notes.evidence: (26) Replacement or adjustment of nonstructural standard fasteners incidental to operations.

notes.front: When may balloon baskets and burners be interchanged on envelopes as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: When designated interchangeable in the type certificate data and designed for quick removal and installation.
notes.explanation: Item (27) of Appendix A(c) sets both conditions.
notes.evidence: (27) The interchange of balloon baskets and burners on envelopes when the basket or burner is designated as interchangeable in the balloon type certificate data and the baskets and burners are specifically designed for quick removal and installation.

notes.front: What three conditions make installing an anti-misfueling device preventive maintenance under item (28)?
notes.back: The device is in the aircraft type certificate data; the manufacturer gave FAA-approved installation instructions; the existing tank filler opening is not disassembled.
notes.explanation: Item (28) covers devices that reduce the diameter of fuel tank filler openings.
notes.evidence: provided the specific device has been made a part of the aircraft type certificiate data by the aircraft manufacturer, the aircraft manufacturer has provided FAA-approved instructions for installation of the specific device, and installation does not involve the disassembly of the existing tank filler opening.

notes.front: Is removing, checking and replacing magnetic chip detectors preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Yes: item (29) of Appendix A(c).
notes.explanation: It is listed without further condition.
notes.evidence: (29) Removing, checking, and replacing magnetic chip detectors.

notes.front: Who may perform the preventive maintenance tasks of an approved primary category aircraft programme under item (30)?
notes.back: At least a private pilot who is the registered owner and holds a certificate of competency for that aircraft.
notes.explanation: The tasks must be those the approved special inspection and preventive maintenance program identifies.
notes.evidence: (i) They are performed by the holder of at least a private pilot certificate issued under part 61 of this chapter who is the registered owner (including co-owners) of the affected aircraft and who holds a certificate of competency for the affected aircraft

notes.front: Under item (31), which panel-mounted units are excluded from removal and replacement as preventive maintenance?
notes.back: Automatic flight control systems, transponders, and microwave frequency distance measuring equipment.
notes.explanation: Item (31) otherwise covers self-contained, tray-mounted navigation and communication devices.
notes.evidence: (excluding automatic flight control systems, transponders, and microwave frequency distance measuring equipment (DME)).

notes.front: After removing and replacing a tray-mounted nav/com unit under item (31), what must be done before its intended use?
notes.back: An operational check in accordance with the applicable sections of part 91.
notes.explanation: The unit must be designed to be readily and repeatedly removed and replaced, with instructions provided.
notes.evidence: The approved unit must be designed to be readily and repeatedly removed and replaced, and pertinent instructions must be provided. Prior to the unit's intended use, and operational check must be performed in accordance with the applicable sections of part 91 of this chapter.

notes.front: An owner-pilot wants to swap the main wheels for skis. The ski installation changes the aircraft's weight and balance, so a computation is needed. How is the job classed?
notes.back: C: not preventive maintenance.
notes.explanation: Item (18) allows the swap as preventive maintenance only where no weight and balance computation is involved.
notes.choices:
A) Preventive maintenance, because wheels and skis are listed
B) Preventive maintenance if a mechanic supervises
C) Not preventive maintenance, because a weight and balance computation is involved
D) A major repair
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the item's condition. B: supervision does not change the classification. D: it is not a repair to structure.
notes.evidence: (18) Replacing wheels and skis where no weight and balance computation is involved.

notes.front: A private owner wants to replace a leaking hydraulic brake hose connection on his aeroplane. Under Appendix A(c), what is this?
notes.back: C: not preventive maintenance.
notes.explanation: Item (21) allows replacing any hose connection except hydraulic connections.
notes.choices:
A) Preventive maintenance
B) Preventive maintenance if the hose is prefabricated
C) Not preventive maintenance: hydraulic connections are excluded
D) A major alteration
notes.choicesExplained: A and B ignore the express exclusion. D: replacing a like hose does not alter the design.
notes.evidence: (21) Replacing any hose connection except hydraulic connections.

notes.front: Under Appendix B(a), in how many copies at least must FAA Form 337 be executed for a major repair or alteration?
notes.back: At least in duplicate.
notes.explanation: Two copies are needed because a signed copy goes to the aircraft owner and a copy is forwarded to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch.
notes.evidence: each person performing a major repair or major alteration shall— (1) Execute FAA Form 337 at least in duplicate; (2) Give a signed copy of that form to the aircraft owner; and

notes.front: Under Appendix B(a)(3), where and when must a copy of Form 337 be forwarded?
notes.back: To the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch in Oklahoma City, within 48 hours after approval for return to service.
notes.explanation: The owner receives the other signed copy.
notes.evidence: Forward a copy of that form to the FAA Aircraft Registration Branch in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, within 48 hours after the aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, or appliance is approved for return to service.

notes.front: A mechanic completes and approves a major alteration for return to service on Monday at 10:00. By when must the FAA copy of Form 337 be forwarded?
notes.back: D: within 48 hours.
notes.explanation: Appendix B counts the 48 hours from approval for return to service.
notes.choices:
A) Within 30 days
B) At the next annual inspection
C) Within 7 days
D) Within 48 hours, by Wednesday at 10:00
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C are not periods Appendix B sets; its limit is 48 hours after approval for return to service.
notes.evidence: within 48 hours after the aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, or appliance is approved for return to service.

notes.front: A certificated repair station makes a major repair following an acceptable manual. What may it use instead of Form 337?
notes.back: The customer's work order, with a signed copy and a signed maintenance release given to the owner.
notes.explanation: This alternative applies to major repairs only, not to major alterations.
notes.evidence: For major repairs made in accordance with a manual or specifications acceptable to the Administrator, a certificated repair station may, in place of the requirements of paragraph (a)— (1) Use the customer's work order upon which the repair is recorded;

notes.front: For extended-range fuel tanks in the passenger or baggage compartment, how many copies of Form 337 are needed, and where does the extra copy go?
notes.back: At least three; one is placed on board the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Section 91.417(d) requires that copy to be kept on board the modified aircraft.
notes.evidence: shall execute an FAA Form 337 in at least triplicate. A completed copy of that form shall be— (1) Placed on board the aircraft as specified in § 91.417 of this chapter;

notes.front: A mechanic plans a major alteration for which no approved data exists. Which item of Form 337 does the FAA complete, and in what case?
notes.back: Item 3, when no approved data exists: the FAA grants a field approval by completing and signing it.
notes.explanation: In many cases it stays blank, because the technician used data already approved by the FAA.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “FAA Form 337—Major Repair and Alteration”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: Item 3 is used when there is no existing approved data for the intended repair or alteration. In that case, the technician can request that the local FSDO Principal Maintenance Inspector (PMI) review the data and then grant a field approval, shown by completing and signing this area.

notes.front: What must item 8 of Form 337, on the reverse side, contain?
notes.back: A description of the work accomplished, including a reference to the approved data used.
notes.explanation: Major repairs and alterations require approved data, and item 8 records which data was used.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “FAA Form 337—Major Repair and Alteration”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: Item 8 (on the reverse side) is for the description of the work accomplished. It must include a reference to the approved data used to conduct the required maintenance.

notes.front: A mechanic arrives to begin a 100-hour inspection. Under Appendix D(a), what must be done before the inspection itself?
notes.back: Remove or open all necessary inspection plates, access doors, fairing and cowling, and thoroughly clean the aircraft and engine.
notes.explanation: The inspection that follows then covers each listed group of components.
notes.evidence: Each person performing an annual or 100-hour inspection shall, before that inspection, remove or open all necessary inspection plates, access doors, fairing, and cowling. He shall thoroughly clean the aircraft and aircraft engine.

notes.front: According to the handbook, how do the Appendix D items differ between an annual and a 100-hour inspection?
notes.back: They do not: the items are exactly the same; the difference is who may perform it and approve return to service.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that section 65.95(a)(2) requires an inspection authorisation holder for the annual.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Appendix D—Scope and Detail of Items”, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: The list of items and areas to be inspected are exactly the same for an annual as a 100-hour inspection. The difference between the inspections is in who is authorized to perform and approve the aircraft for RTS following the inspection.

notes.front: How many specific areas does the handbook say Appendix D identifies for detailed inspection?
notes.back: Eight.
notes.explanation: They are fuselage and hull, cabin and flight deck, engine and nacelle, landing gear, wing and centre section, empennage, propeller and radio.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Appendix D—Scope and Detail of Items”, p. 2-20
notes.evidence: There are eight specific areas identified for detailed inspection. They are the fuselage hull group, cabin/ flight deck group, engine/nacelle group, landing gear group, wing/center section group, empennage assembly, propeller group, and the radio group.

notes.front: In the Appendix D engine and nacelle group, what is the internal engine checked for?
notes.back: Cylinder compression, and metal particles or foreign matter on screens and sump drain plugs.
notes.explanation: Weak compression leads on to checking internal condition and tolerances.
notes.evidence: Internal engine—for cylinder compression and for metal particles or foreign matter on screens and sump drain plugs. If there is weak cylinder compression, for improper internal condition and improper internal tolerances.

notes.front: Under Appendix E(a), what are two checks made on the static pressure system during the altimeter system test?
notes.back: Any two of: freedom from entrapped moisture and restrictions; a proof test of integrity; static port heater operative; no surface changes affecting static pressure.
notes.explanation: Appendix E sets out the tests that section 91.411 requires.
notes.evidence: (1) Ensure freedom from entrapped moisture and restrictions. (2) Perform a proof test to demonstrate the integrity of the static pressure system in a manner acceptable to the Administrator.

notes.front: How may the transponder tests of Appendix F be conducted?
notes.back: Using a bench check or portable test equipment.
notes.explanation: They must meet paragraphs (a) through (j) of the appendix.
notes.evidence: may be conducted using a bench check or portable test equipment and must meet the requirements prescribed in paragraphs (a) through (j) of this appendix.

notes.front: A mechanic signs off an oil change. Weeks later the owner flies the aircraft with an AD overdue. Under 91.403(a), who holds primary responsibility for the aircraft being airworthy?
notes.back: C: the owner or operator.
notes.explanation: Section 91.403(a) puts primary responsibility, including AD compliance, on the owner or operator.
notes.choices:
A) The mechanic who last signed the logbook
B) The FAA inspector for the area
C) The owner or operator
D) The engine manufacturer
notes.choicesExplained: A: a 43.9 signature covers only the work performed. B and D are not given this responsibility by 91.403(a).
notes.evidence: The owner or operator of an aircraft is primarily responsible for maintaining that aircraft in an airworthy condition, including compliance with part 39 of this chapter.

notes.front: Under section 91.403(d), when may a person alter an aircraft based on an STC?
notes.back: Only if the owner or operator holds the STC or has written permission from the holder.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that possessing the STC document does not give rights to its design data.
notes.evidence: A person must not alter an aircraft based on a supplemental type certificate unless the owner or operator of the aircraft is the holder of the supplemental type certificate, or has written permission from the holder.

notes.front: Under section 91.405(a), what must the owner or operator have done between required inspections?
notes.back: Have discrepancies repaired as prescribed in part 43.
notes.explanation: The exception is inoperative items permitted by 91.213(d)(2), which may wait until the next required inspection.
notes.evidence: Shall have that aircraft inspected as prescribed in subpart E of this part and shall between required inspections, except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section, have discrepancies repaired as prescribed in part 43 of this chapter;

notes.front: An owner is flying with an instrument deferred as inoperative under section 91.213(d)(2). By when must it be repaired, replaced, removed or inspected?
notes.back: At the next required inspection.
notes.explanation: Until then, 91.405(d) makes the owner ensure the item is placarded as 43.11 requires.
notes.evidence: Shall have any inoperative instrument or item of equipment, permitted to be inoperative by § 91.213(d)(2) of this part, repaired, replaced, removed, or inspected at the next required inspection; and

notes.front: Under section 91.407(a), what two things must be true before anyone operates an aircraft after maintenance or alteration?
notes.back: It has been approved for return to service by a 43.7 person, and the 43.9 or 43.11 record entry has been made.
notes.explanation: This ties the operating rule in part 91 to the approval and record rules of part 43.
notes.evidence: (1) It has been approved for return to service by a person authorized under § 43.7 of this chapter; and (2) The maintenance record entry required by § 43.9 or § 43.11, as applicable, of this chapter has been made.

notes.front: Under 91.407(b), who must fly an aircraft whose maintenance may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics, before passengers are carried?
notes.back: An appropriately rated pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate, who checks the work and logs the flight in the aircraft records.
notes.explanation: Until then no person other than crewmembers may be carried.
notes.evidence: until an appropriately rated pilot with at least a private pilot certificate flies the aircraft, makes an operational check of the maintenance performed or alteration made, and logs the flight in the aircraft records.

notes.front: After rigging work, ground tests and inspection show conclusively that the aircraft's flight characteristics have not appreciably changed. Is the 91.407(b) test flight still needed?
notes.back: C: no test flight is needed.
notes.explanation: Section 91.407(c) waives the flight when ground tests, inspection or both show conclusively that flight characteristics are unaffected.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, but a mechanic may fly it without a pilot certificate
B) Yes: a test flight is always required after rigging
C) No: conclusive ground tests or inspection remove the need
D) Only if passengers are to be carried within 30 days
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores 91.407(c). A: when a flight is needed, the pilot must hold at least a private certificate. D invents a time limit.
notes.evidence: The aircraft does not have to be flown as required by paragraph (b) of this section if, prior to flight, ground tests, inspection, or both show conclusively that the maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration has not appreciably changed the flight characteristics

notes.front: An aeroplane's annual inspection was signed off on 3 March 2025. Counting 12 calendar months, what is the last day it may be operated without a new annual?
notes.back: A: 31 March 2026.
notes.explanation: Section 91.409(a) counts the preceding 12 calendar months, so the whole of March 2026 is still within the period.
notes.choices:
A) 31 March 2026
B) 28 February 2026
C) 3 March 2026
D) 31 December 2025
notes.choicesExplained: C counts 12 months to the same date instead of to the end of the month. B treats March 2025 as the first of the 12 months. D ends the period at the calendar year, which the rule does not do.
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had— (1) An annual inspection in accordance with part 43 of this chapter

notes.front: When may a 100-hour inspection count as the required annual inspection under 91.409(a)?
notes.back: Only if a person authorised to perform annual inspections does it and it is entered as an "annual" in the records.
notes.explanation: Otherwise a 100-hour inspection cannot substitute for the annual.
notes.evidence: No inspection performed under paragraph (b) of this section may be substituted for any inspection required by this paragraph unless it is performed by a person authorized to perform annual inspections and is entered as an “annual” inspection in the required maintenance records.

notes.front: By how much may the 100-hour limit be exceeded, and for what purpose?
notes.back: By not more than 10 hours, while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done.
notes.explanation: The excess time must be included in computing the next 100 hours.
notes.evidence: The 100-hour limitation may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours while en route to reach a place where the inspection can be done. The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done must be included in computing the next 100 hours of time in service.

notes.front: A rental aeroplane reaches its 100-hour inspection 6 hours late while ferrying to the inspecting shop. After inspection, when is the next 100-hour inspection due?
notes.back: D: 94 hours after the inspection.
notes.explanation: The 6 hours of excess must be included in computing the next 100 hours, leaving 94.
notes.choices:
A) 100 hours after the inspection
B) 106 hours after the inspection
C) 110 hours after the inspection
D) 94 hours after the inspection
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the rule that the excess counts. B adds the excess instead of subtracting it. C treats the 10-hour allowance as a new interval.
notes.evidence: The excess time used to reach a place where the inspection can be done must be included in computing the next 100 hours of time in service.

notes.front: A flight instructor is paid to teach a student in the student's own aeroplane, which the instructor does not provide. No one else is carried for hire. Does 91.409(b) require a 100-hour inspection?
notes.back: A: no.
notes.explanation: The 100-hour rule covers flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides.
notes.choices:
A) No, because the instructor does not provide the aircraft
B) Yes, because instruction is given for hire
C) Yes, because a student is carried
D) Only if the aircraft exceeds 12,500 lb
notes.choicesExplained: B and C miss that the instruction rule covers only aircraft the instructor provides, and the student is not carried for hire. D invents a weight test.
notes.evidence: no person may give flight instruction for hire in an aircraft which that person provides, unless within the preceding 100 hours of time in service the aircraft has received an annual or 100-hour inspection

notes.front: What are two kinds of aircraft to which the 91.409(a) and (b) annual and 100-hour rules do not apply?
notes.back: Any two of: one with a special flight permit; a current experimental certificate; a light-sport special certificate; a provisional certificate.
notes.explanation: Aircraft on certain approved or progressive inspection programs are also excepted.
notes.evidence: An aircraft that carries a special flight permit, a current experimental airworthiness certificate, a special airworthiness certificate in the light-sport category, or provisional airworthiness certificate;

notes.front: Under 91.409(d)(1), who may supervise or conduct a progressive inspection?
notes.back: A certificated mechanic with an inspection authorisation, a certificated airframe repair station, or the aircraft manufacturer.
notes.explanation: The owner or operator must provide one of these when requesting a progressive program.
notes.evidence: A certificated mechanic holding an inspection authorization, a certificated airframe repair station, or the manufacturer of the aircraft to supervise or conduct the progressive inspection;

notes.front: After a progressive inspection is discontinued, when is the first annual inspection due?
notes.back: Within 12 calendar months after the last complete inspection under the progressive program.
notes.explanation: The 100-hour inspection is due within 100 hours after that complete inspection.
notes.evidence: After the discontinuance, the first annual inspection under § 91.409(a)(1) is due within 12 calendar months after the last complete inspection of the aircraft under the progressive inspection. The 100-hour inspection under § 91.409(b) is due within 100 hours after that complete inspection.

notes.front: On a progressive program, the aircraft gets a routine inspection and a detailed inspection of several components. Is that a "complete inspection" for working out when the annual falls due?
notes.back: C: no.
notes.explanation: The rule says a routine inspection plus a detailed inspection of several components is not a complete inspection.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, any detailed inspection counts
B) Yes, if an inspection authorisation holder signs it
C) No: a complete inspection needs a detailed inspection of the aircraft and all its components
D) No, only an annual can be a complete inspection
notes.choicesExplained: A and B ignore the rule's express statement. D: the rule defines a complete inspection within the progressive program itself.
notes.evidence: A complete inspection of the aircraft, for the purpose of determining when the annual and 100-hour inspections are due, requires a detailed inspection of the aircraft and all its components in accordance with the progressive inspection. A routine inspection of the aircraft and a detailed inspection of several components is not considered to be a complete inspection.

notes.front: Under section 91.411, within what period must the static system, altimeters and altitude reporting system have been tested for flight under instrument flight rules in controlled airspace?
notes.back: Within the preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.explanation: They must be found to comply with Appendices E and F of part 43.
notes.evidence: Within the preceding 24 calendar months, each static pressure system, each altimeter instrument, and each automatic pressure altitude reporting system has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendices E and F of part 43 of this chapter;

notes.front: An airframe-rated mechanic without a repair station is asked to do the full section 91.411 test. Which part of it may he perform?
notes.back: Only the static pressure system tests and inspections.
notes.explanation: The other tests are for the aircraft manufacturer or a suitably rated repair station.
notes.evidence: A certificated mechanic with an airframe rating (static pressure system tests and inspections only).

notes.front: Under section 91.413, within what period must a required air traffic control transponder have been tested and inspected?
notes.back: Within the preceding 24 calendar months.
notes.explanation: It must be found to comply with Appendix F of part 43.
notes.evidence: unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, the ATC transponder has been tested and inspected and found to comply with appendix F of part 43 of this chapter;

notes.front: A certificated airframe and powerplant mechanic without a repair station offers to do the 24-month transponder test. Under 91.413(c), may he?
notes.back: D: no.
notes.explanation: Section 91.413(c) lists no mechanic certificate among those who may conduct the transponder tests.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, with an airframe rating
B) Yes, if he holds an inspection authorisation
C) Yes, if supervised by the aircraft owner
D) No: the list is a suitably rated repair station, a continuous-programme holder, or the aircraft manufacturer that installed the transponder
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses this with the 91.411 static system test. B and C add authorities the rule does not give.
notes.evidence: (1) A certificated repair station properly equipped to perform those functions and holding— (i) A radio rating, Class III;

notes.front: Under 91.417(a)(1), which three items must the owner's records of maintenance, alterations and inspections include?
notes.back: A description of the work (or reference to acceptable data), the completion date, and the signature and certificate number of the approver.
notes.explanation: These records cover each aircraft, engine, propeller, rotor and appliance.
notes.evidence: (i) A description (or reference to data acceptable to the Administrator) of the work performed; and (ii) The date of completion of the work performed; and (iii) The signature, and certificate number of the person approving the aircraft for return to service.

notes.front: Which total times must the 91.417(a)(2) records show?
notes.back: The total time in service of the airframe, each engine, each propeller, and each rotor.
notes.explanation: These (a)(2) records are retained and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold.
notes.evidence: (i) The total time in service of the airframe, each engine, each propeller, and each rotor.

notes.front: What must the 91.417(a)(2) records show about life-limited parts?
notes.back: The current status of life-limited parts of each airframe, engine, propeller, rotor and appliance.
notes.explanation: This lets a buyer see how much life remains on each limited part.
notes.evidence: (ii) The current status of life-limited parts of each airframe, engine, propeller, rotor, and appliance.

notes.front: Which overhaul information must the 91.417(a)(2) records contain?
notes.back: The time since last overhaul of all installed items required to be overhauled on a specified time basis.
notes.explanation: Items with no time-based overhaul requirement are not included.
notes.evidence: (iii) The time since last overhaul of all items installed on the aircraft which are required to be overhauled on a specified time basis.

notes.front: What inspection information must the 91.417(a)(2) records contain?
notes.back: The current inspection status, including the time since the last inspection required by the aircraft's inspection program.
notes.explanation: The program is the one under which the aircraft and its appliances are maintained.
notes.evidence: (iv) The current inspection status of the aircraft, including the time since the last inspection required by the inspection program under which the aircraft and its appliances are maintained.

notes.front: An owner complies with a recurring AD. For that AD, what must the section 91.417(a)(2)(v) records show?
notes.back: The method of compliance, the AD number and revision date, and for recurring action the time and date of the next action.
notes.explanation: This is part of the permanent records transferred with the aircraft.
notes.evidence: (v) The current status of applicable airworthiness directives (AD) including, for each, the method of compliance, the AD number and revision date. If the AD involves recurring action, the time and date when the next action is required.

notes.front: Which forms must the 91.417(a)(2) records include copies of?
notes.back: The forms prescribed by 43.9(d) for each major alteration to the airframe and currently installed engines, rotors, propellers and appliances.
notes.explanation: Section 43.9(d) forms are FAA Form 337 under Appendix B.
notes.evidence: (vi) Copies of the forms prescribed by § 43.9(d) of this chapter for each major alteration to the airframe and currently installed engines, rotors, propellers, and appliances.

notes.front: How long must 91.417(a)(1) records be retained?
notes.back: Until the work is repeated or superseded by other work, or for 1 year after the work is performed.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls these temporary records.
notes.evidence: The records specified in paragraph (a)(1) of this section shall be retained until the work is repeated or superseded by other work or for 1 year after the work is performed.

notes.front: How long must 91.417(a)(2) records be retained?
notes.back: They are retained and transferred with the aircraft when it is sold.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls these permanent records.
notes.evidence: The records specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section shall be retained and transferred with the aircraft at the time the aircraft is sold.

notes.front: How long must the owner keep a list of defects furnished under 43.11?
notes.back: Until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service.
notes.explanation: Section 91.417(b)(3) sets this period.
notes.evidence: A list of defects furnished to a registered owner or operator under § 43.11 of this chapter shall be retained until the defects are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service.

notes.front: An owner sells her aeroplane. Which records must, at the least, be transferred with it under 91.417(b)(2)?
notes.back: D: the (a)(2) records.
notes.explanation: Section 91.417(b)(2) requires the (a)(2) records to be retained and transferred with the aircraft at the time it is sold.
notes.choices:
A) Only the last annual inspection entry
B) None; records stay with the seller
C) Only the records less than 1 year old
D) The (a)(2) records, such as total time, life-limited part status and AD status
notes.choicesExplained: A and C describe temporary records, which are not the ones 91.417(b)(2) names. B contradicts the rule.
notes.evidence: The records specified in paragraph (a)(2) of this section shall be retained and transferred with the aircraft at the time the aircraft is sold.

notes.front: When must a copy of FAA Form 337 be kept on board the aircraft?
notes.back: When a fuel tank is installed within the passenger compartment or a baggage compartment under part 43.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes this is the only case where maintenance records must be carried on the aircraft.
notes.evidence: When a fuel tank is installed within the passenger compartment or a baggage compartment pursuant to part 43 of this chapter, a copy of FAA Form 337 shall be kept on board the modified aircraft by the owner or operator.

notes.front: In the handbook's terms, what is the difference between temporary and permanent maintenance records?
notes.back: Temporary (a)(1) records are kept until work is repeated, superseded or 1 year passes; permanent (a)(2) records stay and transfer with the aircraft.
notes.explanation: Permanent records include total time, life-limited part status, overhaul times, inspection status, AD status and major alteration forms.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Temporary Records / Permanent Records”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: These are records that must be kept by the owner until the work is repeated, superseded, or 1 year has transpired since the work was performed.

notes.front: According to the handbook, which change in maintenance documentation has been the most revolutionary of the last 25 years?
notes.back: The introduction of electronic data and record retention.
notes.explanation: Technicians first wrote their own programs for data such as TCDSs and AD notes, before commercial programs appeared.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Electronic Records”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: Nowhere is that change seen as revolutionary as the introduction of electronic data and record retention.

notes.front: A mechanic makes a minor alteration to an appliance. According to the handbook, must a maintenance record entry be created, and for what work in general?
notes.back: Yes: an entry is needed whenever maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding or alteration work occurs on any aircraft item.
notes.explanation: Sections 43.9 and 43.11 set the entries; section 91.417 sets how long they are kept.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Making Maintenance Record Entries”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: Whenever maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration work occurs on an aircraft, airframe, aircraft engine, propeller, appliance, or component part, a maintenance record entry must be created.

notes.front: Under 91.213(a)(2), what do the MEL and the letter of authorisation together constitute?
notes.back: A supplemental type certificate for the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The letter comes from the responsible Flight Standards office and must be in the aircraft.
notes.evidence: The Minimum Equipment List and the letter of authorization constitute a supplemental type certificate for the aircraft.

notes.front: Which three kinds of instruments and equipment may not be included in an MEL?
notes.back: Items essential for safe operation under the type certification rules; items an AD requires operable; items part 91 requires for specific operations.
notes.explanation: The MEL must be prepared within these limitations.
notes.evidence: The following instruments and equipment may not be included in a Minimum Equipment List: (1) Instruments and equipment that are either specifically or otherwise required by the airworthiness requirements under which the aircraft is type certificated and which are essential for safe operations under all operating conditions.

notes.front: Under 91.213(d)(3), what are the two ways to deal with a deferrable inoperative item?
notes.back: Remove it, placard the cockpit control and record under 43.9; or deactivate it and placard it "Inoperative".
notes.explanation: If deactivation involves maintenance, it must be done and recorded under part 43.
notes.evidence: (i) Removed from the aircraft, the cockpit control placarded, and the maintenance recorded in accordance with § 43.9 of this chapter; or (ii) Deactivated and placarded “Inoperative.”

notes.front: Under 91.213(d)(4), who may determine that an inoperative item does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft?
notes.back: An appropriately rated pilot certificated under part 61, or a person certificated and appropriately rated to maintain the aircraft.
notes.explanation: An aircraft so handled is considered in a properly altered condition acceptable to the Administrator.
notes.evidence: A determination is made by a pilot, who is certificated and appropriately rated under part 61 of this chapter, or by a person, who is certificated and appropriately rated to perform maintenance on the aircraft, that the inoperative instrument or equipment does not constitute a hazard to the aircraft.

notes.front: On a piston single with no MEL, the landing light fails before a day flight. It is not equipment required for day visual-flight certification, not on any equipment list, not required by 91.205, and no AD applies. What must happen before take-off?
notes.back: A: remove or deactivate, placard, and make a hazard determination.
notes.explanation: Section 91.213(d) allows the flight once the item is removed or deactivated, placarded, and judged not to be a hazard.
notes.choices:
A) Remove or deactivate it, placard it, and have a pilot or mechanic decide it is no hazard
B) Obtain a special flight permit
C) Nothing; it can simply be ignored
D) Have a Form 337 approved
notes.choicesExplained: C ignores 91.213(d)(3) and (4). B is one option but not required when (d) is met. D is for major repairs and alterations.
notes.evidence: (i) Removed from the aircraft, the cockpit control placarded, and the maintenance recorded in accordance with § 43.9 of this chapter; or (ii) Deactivated and placarded “Inoperative.”

notes.front: In 91.213(d)(1), what distinguishes a master minimum equipment list from an aircraft's own approved MEL?
notes.back: An approved MEL is for one specific aircraft and needs a letter of authorisation; a master list is developed for a kind of aircraft.
notes.explanation: The difference matters because 91.213(d) lets some kinds of aircraft fly without an approved MEL, depending on whether a master list has been developed for them.
notes.evidence: Small rotorcraft, nonturbine-powered small airplane, glider, or lighter-than-air aircraft for which a Master Minimum Equipment List has been developed; and

notes.front: Where must the airworthiness certificate be displayed under 91.203(b)?
notes.back: At the cabin or cockpit entrance, so that it is legible to passengers or crew.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that the certificate must also be on board under 91.203(a)(1).
notes.evidence: is displayed at the cabin or cockpit entrance so that it is legible to passengers or crew.

notes.front: Under 91.203(a)(2), which registration document must be in a civil aircraft operated in the United States?
notes.back: An effective United States registration certificate, or for United States operation the second copy of the registration application.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the application copy the pink copy.
notes.evidence: An effective U.S. registration certificate issued to its owner or, for operation within the United States, the second copy of the Aircraft registration Application as provided for in § 47.31(c),

notes.front: A new owner has sent the registration application but has no certificate yet. How long may the aircraft fly in the United States on the application copy?
notes.back: Up to 90 days, when carried with a current airworthiness certificate or special flight permit.
notes.explanation: The application is FAA Form 8050-1.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Aircraft Registration”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: When carried in the aircraft with an appropriate current airworthiness certificate or a special flight permit, a copy of this completed application provides authority to operate the aircraft in the United States for up to 90 days.

notes.front: An aircraft is later found no longer to conform to its type design. According to the handbook, what can the FAA do with its airworthiness certificate, and why?
notes.back: Revoke it: the certificate rests on conformity to type design and condition for safe operation.
notes.explanation: The certificate is obtained by inspection against those same two requirements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Airworthiness Certificates”, p. 2-37
notes.evidence: Since the ability to obtain this certificate is based upon the requirement to inspect the aircraft to determine that it conforms to type design and is in condition for safe operation, it can also be revoked by the FAA if either of those two requirements ceases to exist.

notes.front: What are two purposes for which a special flight permit may be issued?
notes.back: Any two of: flying to a base for repairs, maintenance or storage; delivering or exporting; production flight testing; evacuating from danger; customer demonstrations.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists these five; the aircraft must still be capable of safe flight.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Special Flight Permits”, p. 10-17
notes.evidence: Flying the aircraft to a base where repairs, alterations, or maintenance are to be performed or to a point of storage • Delivering or exporting the aircraft • Production flight testing new production aircraft • Evacuating aircraft from areas of impending danger

notes.front: An aeroplane is not in compliance with an AD and cannot legally be flown. The owner wants to fly it to a shop to have the AD work done. The operator has no operations specifications. What does part 39 say?
notes.back: D: a special flight permit, unless the AD says otherwise.
notes.explanation: Section 39.23 lets the FAA issue a special flight permit to reach a repair facility, and it may add requirements or decline if the move is unsafe.
notes.choices:
A) Only an AMOC can allow the flight
B) The aircraft must be dismantled and trucked
C) It may be flown freely for up to 10 hours
D) The FAA may issue a special flight permit unless the AD states otherwise
notes.choicesExplained: B is not required. C confuses this with the 100-hour overrun. A: an AMOC is a different way to address the unsafe condition, not a ferry authority.
notes.evidence: If you do not have this authority, the local Flight Standards District Office of FAA may issue you a special flight permit unless the airworthiness directive states otherwise.

notes.front: A mechanic keeps finding the same mechanical difficulty on one aircraft type and files a Malfunction or Defect Report. According to the handbook, what do such reports contribute to?
notes.back: The correction of conditions that would otherwise keep proving costly or adversely affect airworthiness.
notes.explanation: They give the FAA and industry a service record of mechanical difficulties.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Glossary: Malfunction or Defect Report”, p. G-6
notes.evidence: Such reports contribute to the correction of conditions or situations which otherwise will continue to prove costly and/or adversely affect the airworthiness of aircraft.

notes.front: Under section 39.5, what two findings lead the FAA to issue an AD?
notes.back: An unsafe condition exists in the product, and it is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
notes.explanation: Both findings are needed; the AD then addresses that product.
notes.evidence: (a) An unsafe condition exists in the product; and (b) The condition is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.

notes.front: Where does the FAA publish ADs in full, and as amendments to which section?
notes.back: In the Federal Register, as amendments to section 39.13.
notes.explanation: ADs are part of the Code of Federal Regulations but are not codified in the annual edition.
notes.evidence: Yes, airworthiness directives are part of the Code of Federal Regulations, but they are not codified in the annual edition. FAA publishes airworthiness directives in full in the Federal Register as amendments to § 39.13.

notes.front: An AD calls for inspecting a wing fitting. The owner's aircraft had that area repaired and modified years ago. Under part 39, what applies?
notes.back: D: the AD still applies; request an AMOC if needed.
notes.explanation: Section 39.15 applies the AD even if the product was modified, altered or repaired in that area; 39.17 then requires an AMOC request if the change affects the required actions.
notes.choices:
A) The AD no longer applies because the area was changed
B) Only the repair station that did the repair must comply
C) The owner may choose to ignore the AD if the repair was approved
D) The AD still applies, and if the change prevents the required actions, an AMOC must be requested
notes.choicesExplained: A and C contradict 39.15. B: the rules on operating a non-compliant product apply to whoever operates it, not the repairer.
notes.evidence: an airworthiness directive applies to each product identified in the airworthiness directive, even if an individual product has been changed by modifying, altering, or repairing it in the area addressed by the airworthiness directive.

notes.front: Under 39.19, to whom do you normally send a proposed AMOC, and who must approve it before use?
notes.back: Your principal inspector; you may use it only if the manager of the office identified in the AD approves it.
notes.explanation: Without a principal inspector, the proposal goes directly to that manager.
notes.evidence: Unless FAA authorizes otherwise, send your proposal to your principal inspector. Include the specific actions you are proposing to address the unsafe condition. The principal inspector may add comments and will send your request to the manager of the office identified in the airworthiness directive (manager).

notes.front: An operator cannot meet an AD's compliance time and proposes an alternative method. Can a different compliance time be approved?
notes.back: Yes, if the revised time with the approved alternative method gives an acceptable level of safety as the AD requires.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that the alternative must accomplish the intent of the AD.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Alternative Method of Compliance”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: A compliance time that differs from the requirements of the AD can also be approved if the revised time period and approved alternative method provides an acceptable level of safety as the requirements of the AD.

notes.front: An AD incorporates a manufacturer's service bulletin by reference but modifies one of its steps. The mechanic finds the two conflict. Which is followed?
notes.back: D: the AD.
notes.explanation: The incorporated service document becomes part of the AD, but where they conflict the AD's requirements govern.
notes.choices:
A) The service bulletin, as the manufacturer's own data
B) Whichever is more conservative
C) Either, at the mechanic's choice
D) The AD
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C ignore 39.27, which resolves any conflict in favour of the AD.
notes.evidence: In these cases, the service document becomes part of the airworthiness directive. In some cases the directions in the service document may be modified by the airworthiness directive. If there is a conflict between the service document and the airworthiness directive, you must follow the requirements of the airworthiness directive.

notes.front: What is the standard AD process?
notes.back: A notice of proposed rulemaking, which invites public comment, followed by a final rule.
notes.explanation: The final rule's preamble responds to substantive comments or states none were received.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Airworthiness Directives (AD)”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: The standard AD process is to issue an NPRM followed by a Final Rule. After an unsafe condition is discovered, a proposed solution is published as an NPRM and solicits public comment on the proposed action.

notes.front: Which type of AD is adopted immediately and published with a request for comments?
notes.back: The Final Rule; Request for Comments (an immediately adopted rule).
notes.explanation: It is used when there is too little time for public comment before the terminating action, that is, less than 60 days.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Airworthiness Directives (AD)”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: If time for the terminating action to be accomplished is too short to allow for public comment (that is, less than 60 days), then a finding of impracticability is justified for the terminating action, and it can be issued as an immediately adopted rule. The immediately adopted rule is published in the Federal Register with a request for comments.

notes.front: An unsafe condition needs immediate action, and the FAA faxes an AD to known owners. What type of AD is this, and to whom is it effective at first?
notes.back: An Emergency AD; it is effective only to the people who actually receive it.
notes.explanation: It may be distributed by fax, letter or other methods, to rapidly correct an urgent safety deficiency.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Types of Airworthiness Directives (AD)”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: An Emergency AD is issued when an unsafe condition exists that requires immediate action by an owner/operator. The intent of an Emergency AD is to rapidly correct an urgent safety deficiency. An Emergency AD may be distributed by fax, letter, or other methods. It is issued and effective to only the people who actually receive it.

notes.front: What are the three parts of an AD number?
notes.back: The calendar year of issuance, the biweekly period of the year when assigned, and a sequential number within that period.
notes.explanation: So two ADs from the same fortnight share their first two parts.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “AD Number”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: ADs have a three-part number designator. The first part is the calendar year of issuance. The second part is the biweekly period of the year when the number is assigned. The third part is issued sequentially within each biweekly period.

notes.front: To find all ADs applicable to a product, what must you search?
notes.back: ADs on the product, aircraft, engines, propeller and any installed appliance, and on the model and its specific series.
notes.explanation: The AD applicability section lists affected models and special considerations such as installed part numbers.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Applicability and Compliance”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: In order to find all applicable ADs for a specific product, you must search for ADs on the product, aircraft, engine(s), propeller, or any installed appliance. If there are multiple series under the aircraft or engine model, you must also search for ADs applicable to the model, as well as the specific series of that model.

notes.front: How does a SAIB differ from an AD?
notes.back: A SAIB carries non-regulatory information and recommendations; an AD is a legally enforceable rule.
notes.explanation: SAIBs cover concerns that do not meet the criteria for an AD.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB)”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: SAIBs contain non-regulatory information and guidance that does not meet the criteria for an AD.

notes.front: A manufacturer issues a service bulletin recommending a new fuel-selector seal. No AD refers to it, and the owner's inspection program does not require it. What is its status for this privately operated aircraft?
notes.back: B: recommended but not mandatory.
notes.explanation: SBs are required only when an AD refers to them or the authorised inspection program requires them.
notes.choices:
A) Mandatory within 100 hours
B) Recommended but not mandatory
C) Mandatory at the next annual inspection
D) Void unless the FAA approves it
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat the SB as an AD. D: SBs are manufacturer information and need no FAA approval to exist.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Service Bulletins (SB)”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: SBs are good information and should be strongly considered by the owner for implementation to the aircraft. However, SBs are not required unless they are referred to in an AD note or if compliance is required as a part of the authorized inspection program.

notes.front: How does a component maintenance manual differ from the AMM?
notes.back: The component manual focuses on one item, such as a hydraulic pump, and usually serves as its overhaul manual; the AMM covers the whole aircraft.
notes.explanation: The component manual gives the bench mechanic detailed troubleshooting information.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Airworthiness Limitations”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: The CMM, on the other hand, is focused on a specific item or component, such as hydraulic pump, generator, or thrust reverser. It provides the bench mechanic with detail troubleshooting information and usually serves as an overhaul manual

notes.front: An aircraft's flight manual is missing from the aircraft. According to the handbook, why can this make the aircraft unairworthy?
notes.back: Flight manuals are usually listed in the aircraft TCDS, so the manual is a required item for the aircraft to be airworthy.
notes.explanation: They give the pilot the information needed to operate the aircraft properly.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Airworthiness Limitations”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: These manuals are usually listed in the aircraft TCDS, and therefore are a required item for the aircraft to be considered airworthy.

notes.front: A technician needs electrical system information in the maintenance manual of an unfamiliar large aircraft. Which ATA chapter should she open?
notes.back: Chapter 24 (Electrical Power).
notes.explanation: Standardisation means a system is in the same section of the maintenance manual whatever the manufacturer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Special Inspections”, p. 10-12
notes.evidence: As a result of this standardization, maintenance technicians can always find information regarding a particular system in the same section of an aircraft maintenance manual, regardless of manufacturer. For example, if seeking information about the electrical system on any aircraft, that information is always found in section (chapter) 24.

notes.front: Before installing an STC modification, which effectivity information in the STC tells a mechanic whether it covers the particular aircraft?
notes.back: Serial number effectivity.
notes.explanation: The STC also defines the design change and states how it affects the existing type design.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Supplemental Type Certificates (STC)”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: The STC defines the product design change, states how the modification affects the existing type design, and lists serial number effectivity.

notes.front: Which risk related to effectivity does the Aviation Mechanic Airman Certification Standards ask applicants to manage?
notes.back: Determination of component applicability to a given aircraft.
notes.explanation: Effectivity codes in parts manuals are how that applicability is shown.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant ACS (FAA-S-ACS-1), Area I, Task I: Regulations, Maintenance Forms, Records, and Publications, p. 14
notes.evidence: AM.I.I.R5 Determination of component applicability to a given aircraft.

notes.front: A technician skips a caution printed in a maintenance manual procedure. Which risk named in the Aviation Mechanic Airman Certification Standards has he failed to manage?
notes.back: Adherence to warnings, cautions, or notes in maintenance and operational manuals.
notes.explanation: The standards also expect knowledge of the basic definition of warnings, cautions and notes.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant ACS (FAA-S-ACS-1), Area I, Task I: Regulations, Maintenance Forms, Records, and Publications, p. 14
notes.evidence: AM.I.I.R4 Adherence to warnings, cautions, or notes in maintenance and operational manuals.

notes.front: What kind of data do minor repairs and alterations need, and how are they recorded?
notes.back: Only "acceptable" data, such as manufacturers' manuals or AC 43.13-1; a logbook entry is enough.
notes.explanation: Major repairs and alterations, by contrast, need "approved data".
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Section 43.5—Approval for return to service”, p. 2-15
notes.evidence: Minor repairs and alterations need only to refer to “acceptable” data, such as manufacturers’ maintenance manuals or AC 43.13-1. The maintenance action can simply be recorded in the maintenance record as a logbook entry.

notes.front: What are three examples of approved data that major repairs and alterations may use, per the handbook?
notes.back: Any three of: AD notes, STCs, TCDS, designated engineering representative delegations, FAA-approved manufacturer service bulletins.
notes.explanation: Minor work needs only acceptable data.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Section 43.5—Approval for return to service”, p. 2-15
notes.evidence: Major repairs and alterations require “approved data.” Some examples of approved data are AD notes, STCs, TCDS, DER-specific delegations, and FAA-approved manufacturer Service Bulletins (SB).

notes.front: A mechanic plans a major repair to a wing spar on a light aeroplane. Which data will support it?
notes.back: B: approved data.
notes.explanation: The handbook says major repairs and alterations require approved data, while minor ones need only acceptable data.
notes.choices:
A) Any acceptable data, such as a general textbook
B) Approved data, such as an STC or FAA-approved manufacturer data
C) No data if the mechanic holds an inspection authorisation
D) Only the pilot's operating handbook
notes.choicesExplained: A is enough only for minor work. C: an authorisation does not replace data. D is operating, not repair, information.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Section 43.5—Approval for return to service”, p. 2-15
notes.evidence: Major repairs and alterations require “approved data.” Some examples of approved data are AD notes, STCs, TCDS, DER-specific delegations, and FAA-approved manufacturer Service Bulletins (SB).

notes.front: What can a technician request when a major repair or alteration has no previously approved data?
notes.back: A field approval from the FAA.
notes.explanation: The technician completes the front of Form 337 through block 6, leaving block 3 open for later FAA approval.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Section 43.5—Approval for return to service”, p. 2-15
notes.evidence: Sometimes the repair or alteration being performed does not have previously-approved data. In that case, the technician may request that the FAA accomplish a “Field Approval.” In this procedure, the technician completes the front side of Form 337 through block 6 (leaving block 3 open for later FAA approval)

notes.front: A shop manager says the methods in an AC are mandatory. When is the content of an AC actually binding on the public?
notes.back: Only when incorporated into a regulation by reference.
notes.explanation: ACs give guidance and do not create or change regulatory requirements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Advisory Circulars (AC)”, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: Unless incorporated into a regulation by reference, the content of ACs are not binding on the public.

notes.front: In an AC number such as 25-42C, what does the first part (25) identify?
notes.back: The subject matter area, which corresponds to the part of the FAA regulations (here part 25).
notes.explanation: ACs are numbered to match the subject areas of the regulations.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “The AC Numbering System”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: The first part of the number identifies the subject matter area of the AC. This corresponds to the part of the FAA’s regulations. In the above example, this would be part 25.

notes.front: A mechanic finds AC 25-42C on the shelf. What does the letter C tell her?
notes.back: The revision sequence: this is the third revision. A first version has no revision letter.
notes.explanation: The letter is assigned by the originating office.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “The AC Numbering System”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: The third part of the number is a letter assigned by the originating office showing the revision sequence if an AC is revised. The first version of an AC does not have a revision letter. In the above example, this is third revision, as designated by the “C.”

notes.front: A mechanic wants AC 43.13-1B repair data to serve as FAA-approved data for a major repair. What must she list in Block 8 of Form 337?
notes.back: The AC chapter, page and paragraph; the data must also meet three conditions.
notes.explanation: The repair must be to a nonpressurised area of a civil aircraft.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, “1. Purpose of this advisory circular”, p. i
notes.evidence: The repair data may be used as FAA-approved data for repairs of nonpressurized areas of civil aircraft provided the AC chapter, page, and paragraph are listed in Block 8 of FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration (Airframe, Powerplant, Propeller, or Appliance) and the data are:

notes.back: Appropriate to the product being repaired.
notes.explanation: All three conditions must be met, with the AC reference in Block 8 of Form 337.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, “1. Purpose of this advisory circular”, p. i
notes.evidence: (1) Appropriate to the product being repaired; (2) Directly applicable to the repair being made; and (3) Not contrary to manufacturer’s data.

notes.front: A mechanic needs the current AC 43.13-1B. Where does the AC itself say it can be found online?
notes.back: On the FAA's advisory circulars web page and in the Dynamic Regulatory System at drs.faa.gov.
notes.explanation: The Dynamic Regulatory System is one of the FAA resources for finding guidance material.
notes.source: AC 43.13-1B Change 1, “3. Where you can find this AC”, p. i
notes.evidence: You can find this AC on the FAA’s website at https://www.faa.gov/regulations_policies/advisory_circulars and the Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) at https://drs.faa.gov.

notes.front: A mechanic obtains a copy of an STC document and wants to install the modification on a customer's aircraft. Is holding the document enough?
notes.back: No: the STC and its data are the holder's property; you must contact the holder for rights to use it.
notes.explanation: Section 91.403(d) likewise requires the holder's written permission.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Supplemental Type Certificates (STC)”, p. 2-30
notes.evidence: Possession of the STC document does not constitute rights to the design data or installation of the modification. The STC and its supporting data (drawings, instructions, specifications, and so forth) are the property of the STC holder. You must contact the STC holder to obtain rights for the use of the STC.

notes.front: What are three things the TCDS lists for the specified product?
notes.back: Any three of: engine make and model, fuel type, engine limits, airspeed limits, maximum weight, minimum crew.
notes.explanation: These are the conditions and limitations under which the airworthiness requirements were met.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Type Certificate Data Sheets (TCDS)”, p. 2-30
notes.evidence: The TCDS lists the specifications, conditions, and limitations that the airworthiness requirements were met under for the specified product, such as engine make and model, fuel type, engine limits, airspeed limits, maximum weight, minimum crew, and so forth.

notes.front: A mechanic must confirm which engine models and fuel grade are approved for an aircraft before an engine change. Which FAA document is the direct source?
notes.back: D: the TCDS.
notes.explanation: The TCDS lists the conditions and limitations of type certification, including engine make and model and fuel type.

B) The certificate of aircraft registration

notes.front: Which three regulations does the handbook call the primary regulations governing an aircraft's airworthiness?
notes.back: Part 21 (certification procedures), part 43 (maintenance and alteration) and part 91 (general operating and flight rules).
notes.explanation: Most other airworthiness regulations link to one of these three.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Overview”, p. 2-2
notes.evidence: 1. 14 CFR part 21—Certification Procedures for Products and Parts 2. 14 CFR part 43—Maintenance, Preventive Maintenance, Rebuilding, and Alterations 3. 14 CFR part 91—General Operating and Flight Rules

notes.front: What maximum certificated takeoff weight applies to part 23 aircraft, and to the commuter category?
notes.back: 12,500 pounds or less; the commuter category rises to 19,000 pounds or less.
notes.explanation: Part 23 covers much of what the industry calls general aviation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “14 CFR Part 23”, p. 2-5
notes.evidence: Part 23 aircraft are those aircraft that have a maximum certificated takeoff weight of 12,500 pounds or less, except for those aircraft in the commuter category. The maximum certificated takeoff weight limit rises to 19,000 pounds or less for these aircraft.

notes.front: Under part 45, what are three items that must appear on the fireproof data plate of a type-certificated product?
notes.back: Any three of: builder's name, model designation, builder's serial number, type certificate number, production certificate number, engine rating, among others.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists eight items in all.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “14 CFR Part 45—Identification and Registration Marking”, p. 2-8
notes.evidence: All type-certificated products must have the following information on a fireproof dataplate or similar approved fireproof method. 1. Builder’s name 2. Model designation 3. Builder’s serial number 4. TC number (if any) 5. Production certificate number (if any)

notes.front: An owner asks why a part 91 operating rule obliges anyone maintaining his aircraft to follow part 43. Which section makes the link?
notes.back: Section 91.403(b): no one may perform maintenance, preventive maintenance or alterations other than as prescribed in that subpart and part 43.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes the direct line from part 91 to part 43 in its chart.
notes.evidence: No person may perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, or alterations on an aircraft other than as prescribed in this subpart and other applicable regulations, including part 43 of this chapter.

notes.front: Under part 147, what are the minimum curriculum hours for airframe or powerplant training alone, and for both?
notes.back: 1,150 hours for either; 1,900 hours for both.
notes.explanation: The 400 hours of general studies are counted only once in the combined total.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “14 CFR Part 147—Aviation Maintenance Technician Schools”, p. 2-13
notes.evidence: The minimum number of curriculum hours for conducting either airframe or powerplant training independently is 1,150. If both A&P ratings are offered, the combined total curriculum hours are 1,900.

notes.front: Is FAA Form 337 required to document major repairs and alterations on light-sport aircraft, per the handbook?
notes.back: No: the work is evaluated against the applicable industry consensus standards, and a written affidavit is provided instead.
notes.explanation: The manufacturer or an entity it approves does the evaluation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Major Repairs & Alterations”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: Another major difference between LSA maintenance and traditional aircraft maintenance is that FAA Form 337, Major Repair and Alteration, is not required to document major repairs and alterations.

notes.front: In the light-sport standard, what is the minimum level of certification to accomplish line maintenance?
notes.back: Light-sport repairman with an inspection rating.
notes.explanation: Typical line tasks include the 100-hour or annual condition inspection and servicing fluids.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Line Maintenance, Repairs, & Alterations”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: The minimum level of certification necessary to accomplish line maintenance is LSA inspection. Some typical tasks considered to be line maintenance are: • 100-hour/annual condition inspection • Servicing of fluids

notes.front: An owner of a special light-sport aircraft wants the fuel pump replaced; the maintenance manual gives instructions for it. Under the standard the handbook reviews, what kind of maintenance is this?
notes.back: B: line maintenance.
notes.explanation: Removing and replacing components such as a fuel pump, with instructions in the manual, is listed as typical line maintenance.
notes.choices:
A) Heavy maintenance
B) Line maintenance
C) A major alteration
D) Overhaul
notes.choicesExplained: A needs manufacturer-designated specialised training or equipment. D is limited to the manufacturer or its authorised party. C changes the design.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (FAA-H-8083-30B), “Line Maintenance, Repairs, & Alterations”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: Removing and replacing components when instructions to do so are provided in the maintenance manual • – Batteries – Fuel pump – Exhaust – Spark plugs and wires – Floats and skis
